summary: This document defines two new RADIUS attributes that carry DHCP options, so a RADIUS server can pass DHCP-related configuration to the device that hands out addresses. It works for both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 and for any service that relies on DHCP. It also updates RFC 4014 by relaxing a restriction on which RADIUS attributes may appear in the DHCP suboption.

eli5.summary: A front desk has a list of rules from the manager. This lets the manager slip extra notes, written in the hotel's own room-key language, onto that list for the desk to hand to guests.

subtitle: Two new RADIUS attributes that carry DHCP options from an authentication server to the device that configures a customer's network.

tldr.problem: ISPs use RADIUS to decide how a customer's connection is configured, but RADIUS had no attribute that could carry arbitrary DHCP options, for example the ones needed to hand out encrypted DNS resolver information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DHCPv6-Options attribute (245.3) and the DHCPv4-Options attribute (245.4), each holding a list of DHCP options. It also updates RFC 4014 so a DHCP relay agent can pass such attributes to a DHCP server.
tldr.outcome: A RADIUS server can now feed any permitted DHCP option into the DHCP exchange with a customer device, with the permitted options and attributes tracked in new IANA registries.

today: RFC 9445 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 4014 by replacing its fixed attribute list with an IANA registry.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needs to Carry DHCP Options
sections.content:
ISPs usually provide DNS resolvers to their customers. They advertise them with mechanisms such as DHCP and IPv6 Router Advertisement, and the information used to fill those messages typically comes from specific RADIUS attributes, such as the DNS-Server-IPv6-Address attribute.

Encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT and DoQ) needs more than a list of addresses. A separate document, referred to in this RFC as [DNR], uses DHCP to give hosts the information needed to reach an encrypted DNS resolver. The problem is that no RADIUS attributes existed that could populate those DHCP messages, and the RFC expects the same gap for future services configured through DHCP.

So the RFC takes a generic route. Instead of one attribute per service, it defines two attributes that wrap whole DHCP options: one for DHCPv6 and one for DHCPv4. Which options go inside can be controlled by a deployment-specific policy, and discussing such a policy is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The network's boss computer knows what settings each customer should get. It had no way to pass along new kinds of settings, so this gives it a general-purpose envelope.

sections.title: The Two New Attributes
sections.content:
Both attributes use the Long Extended Type format from RFC 6929, so they can carry more than 253 octets of data. Both have type 245 and are of type string. DHCPv6-Options has Extended-Type 3 (identifier 245.3), and DHCPv4-Options has Extended-Type 4 (identifier 245.4).

The Value field holds a list of DHCP options. Multiple instances of the same DHCPv6 option may appear, and each is treated as separate: the data areas MUST NOT be concatenated or combined. For DHCPv4, multiple instances are allowed especially for options that exceed the maximum DHCPv4 option size of 255 octets, and the mechanism in RFC 3396 MUST be used to split and join them.

Each attribute MAY appear in an Access-Accept, a CoA-Request and an Accounting-Request. It MAY also appear in an Access-Request as a hint about the client's preference, which the server is not required to honor. It MUST NOT appear in any other RADIUS packet.
sections.eli5: There are two envelopes, one for the newer kind of address settings and one for the older kind. Each envelope can hold lots of little setting cards.

sections.title: Size Limits, Precedence and Permitted Options
sections.content:
DHCP options inside these attributes are limited by the RADIUS maximum packet size of 4096 bytes. For deployments with large options, implementations are RECOMMENDED to support a packet size up to 65535 bytes, for example through the mechanisms in RFC 7499 or RFC 7930. The values are encoded in the clear and are not encrypted like the Tunnel-Password attribute.

Implementations may offer configuration to control which DHCP options can be included. Absent explicit configuration, RADIUS and DHCP server implementations SHOULD ignore non-permitted DHCP options received in these attributes. The permitted options are listed in two new IANA registries, whose initial entries are the encrypted DNS options: OPTION_V6_DNR (144) for DHCPv6 and OPTION_V4_DNR (tag 162) for DHCPv4.

Because RADIUS data is returned as a result of authentication and authorization checks, and absent explicit configuration on the DHCP server, it takes precedence over any local configuration.
sections.eli5: The envelopes can be big, but they are not locked, so the desk only follows note types it has been told to trust. When the boss and the desk disagree, the boss's note wins.

sections.title: Updating RFC 4014 for DHCP Relay Agents
sections.content:
RFC 4014 lets a DHCPv4 relay agent pass RADIUS attributes it received during authentication to a DHCPv4 server, using the RADIUS Attributes DHCP suboption. That RFC fixed a short list of allowed attributes, which does not suit new services such as encrypted DNS.

This RFC updates Sections 3 and 4 of RFC 4014. The relay agent SHOULD only include attributes from the new IANA registry "RADIUS Attributes Permitted in RADIUS Attributes DHCP Suboption", and may support a configuration parameter for this. A DHCP server SHOULD ignore relayed attributes not in that registry when explicit configuration is absent.

The registry starts with seven entries: User-Name (1), Service-Type (6), Vendor-Specific (26), Session-Timeout (27), Framed-Pool (88), Framed-IPv6-Pool (100) and DHCPv4-Options (245.4). Its allocation policy is Expert Review. For DHCPv6 relays, RFC 7037 already provides a similar path, and DHCPv6-Options (245.3) was added to the matching registry.
sections.eli5: The messenger who carries notes between the boss and the desk used to be allowed to carry only a short fixed list of note types. Now the list can grow, as long as the new types are registered.

sections.title: Example: Encrypted DNS Provisioning
sections.content:
The RFC shows a Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) that gets an encrypted DNS resolver. The Network Access Server (NAS) acts as both RADIUS client and DHCPv6 server. When the CPE sends a DHCPv6 Solicit, the NAS sends a RADIUS Access-Request to the AAA server. The Access-Accept carries OPTION_V6_DNR instances inside the DHCPv6-Options attribute, and the NAS uses them in its DHCPv6 Advertise and Reply messages.

If the encrypted DNS information changes, the RADIUS server sends a Change-of-Authorization (CoA) message carrying the updated option. After validating it, the NAS replies with a CoA ACK, replaces the old information and sends a DHCPv6 Reconfigure message, which leads the client to start a Renew/Reply exchange.

A second example uses DHCPv4 the same way, with OPTION_V4_DNR flowing through DHCPDISCOVER, DHCPOFFER, DHCPREQUEST and DHCPACK. The RFC adds that other scenarios, such as returning different DoH URI Templates depending on service and policy, can be envisaged.
sections.eli5: A new customer asks the desk for settings. The desk checks with the boss, gets the settings, and passes them on. If the boss changes the settings later, the desk tells the customer to ask again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the existing security discussions for RADIUS, DHCPv6 and DHCPv4, and says that risks specific to each DHCP option are covered by the documents defining those options.

RADIUS servers have conventionally accepted arbitrary data in string attributes, letting administrators hand-craft opaque content. It is RECOMMENDED that servers implementing this specification understand the format and encoding of DHCP options, so administrators can enter options as options rather than as encoded strings. The RFC says this improves security, interoperability and usability.

Where relay agents pass the attributes on to DHCP servers, the considerations in RFC 4014 and RFC 7037 should be taken into account, as should the Reconfigure-related considerations in RFC 6977.
sections.eli5: Writing the settings by hand as a long string of secret code makes mistakes easy. It is safer when the boss's computer understands the settings and writes the code itself.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned the two attribute types, 245.3 (DHCPv6-Options) and 245.4 (DHCPv4-Options), both of data type string. It added 245.3 to the existing "RADIUS Attributes Permitted in DHCPv6 RADIUS Option" registry.

It also created three new Expert Review registries: the DHCP suboption attributes registry described above, "DHCPv6 Options Permitted in the RADIUS DHCPv6-Options Attribute" and "DHCP Options Permitted in the RADIUS DHCPv4-Options Attribute".

The RFC suggests several designated experts. They check that a request does not duplicate an existing entry and that its description is clear. Requests go to a review list and are evaluated within a three-week review period.
sections.eli5: The official list keeper wrote down the two new envelope names and started three new sign-up sheets for which note types are allowed.
